solution:
A chemical bond is formed because atoms tend to acquire the stable outer-shell configuration of the nearest noble gas — an octet of electrons (a duplet for hydrogen and helium). Atoms achieve this in two ways.

**By transfer of electrons (ionic or electrovalent bond).** An atom of low ionization enthalpy loses one or more valence electrons and an atom with a high negative electron gain enthalpy accepts them. Both the ions formed attain a noble-gas configuration, and the oppositely charged ions are then held together by electrostatic attraction:

\(\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + e^-\); \(\text{Cl} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-\); \(\text{Na}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{NaCl}\)

**By sharing of electrons (covalent bond).** Each combining atom contributes at least one electron to a shared pair, and both atoms count the shared pair towards their own octet. In \(\text{Cl}_2\) each chlorine atom contributes one electron to a single shared pair, so each attains the argon configuration.

Sharing one pair gives a single bond, two pairs a double bond (as in \(\text{CO}_2\)) and three pairs a triple bond (as in \(\text{N}_2\)).

In a Lewis dot symbol the chemical symbol stands for the kernel (nucleus plus inner electrons) and the number of dots around it equals the number of valence electrons. So first write the outer-shell configuration of each atom and count its valence electrons:

- Mg — \([\text{Ne}]3s^2\), 2 valence electrons → 2 dots
- Na — \([\text{Ne}]3s^1\), 1 valence electron → 1 dot
- B — \([\text{He}]2s^2\,2p^1\), 3 valence electrons → 3 dots
- O — \([\text{He}]2s^2\,2p^4\), 6 valence electrons → 6 dots (two lone pairs and two single electrons)
- N — \([\text{He}]2s^2\,2p^3\), 5 valence electrons → 5 dots (one lone pair and three single electrons)
- Br — \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2\,4p^5\), 7 valence electrons → 7 dots (three lone pairs and one single electron)

The dots are placed singly on the four sides of the symbol first and only then paired up.

Number of dots: Mg 2, Na 1, B 3, O 6, N 5, Br 7.

For an anion add one dot for each unit of negative charge; for a cation remove one dot for each unit of positive charge, and enclose the ion in square brackets with its charge written outside.

**S and \(\text{S}^{2-}\).** S is \([\text{Ne}]3s^2\,3p^4\), so the Lewis symbol carries 6 dots. \(\text{S}^{2-}\) has gained 2 electrons, so it carries 8 dots (four lone pairs) and is written \([\,\ddot{\text{S}}\,]^{2-}\) with the argon octet complete.

**Al and \(\text{Al}^{3+}\).** Al is \([\text{Ne}]3s^2\,3p^1\), so the Lewis symbol carries 3 dots. \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) has lost all three valence electrons, so it carries NO dots and is written \([\text{Al}]^{3+}\); its outer shell is now the neon configuration.

**H and \(\text{H}^-\).** H has 1 valence electron, so 1 dot. \(\text{H}^-\) has gained one electron and carries 2 dots, \([\text{H}:]^-\) — the helium duplet, not an octet.

Dots: S 6, \(\text{S}^{2-}\) 8, Al 3, \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) 0, H 1, \(\text{H}^-\) 2.

In each case add the valence electrons of the combining atoms (adding one electron per unit of negative charge), place the least electronegative atom at the centre, join the atoms by single bonds and then distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs or multiple bonds so that every bonded atom reaches an octet (a duplet for H).

**\(\text{H}_2\text{S}\)** — \(6 + 2(1) = 8\) electrons. S is central; two S–H single bonds use 4 electrons, and the remaining 4 sit on sulphur as two lone pairs.

**\(\text{SiCl}_4\)** — \(4 + 4(7) = 32\) electrons. Si is central; four Si–Cl single bonds use 8 electrons, and the remaining 24 are three lone pairs on each chlorine.

**\(\text{BeF}_2\)** — \(2 + 2(7) = 16\) electrons. Be is central; two Be–F single bonds use 4 electrons and the remaining 12 are three lone pairs on each fluorine. Beryllium is left with only four electrons — this is an example of the incomplete octet of the central atom.

**\(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\)** — \(4 + 3(6) + 2 = 24\) electrons. C is central; one C=O double bond and two C–O single bonds. The two singly bonded oxygens carry three lone pairs each and one unit of negative charge each; the doubly bonded oxygen carries two lone pairs. The whole ion is enclosed in brackets with the charge \(2-\) outside.

**HCOOH** — \(2(1) + 4 + 2(6) = 18\) electrons. The skeleton is H–C(=O)–O–H: a C–H single bond, a C=O double bond (that oxygen keeping two lone pairs), a C–O single bond and an O–H single bond (that oxygen also keeping two lone pairs). Carbon then has four bonds and an octet.

**Octet rule.** Atoms combine either by transferring valence electrons from one atom to another (gaining or losing them) or by sharing valence electrons, so as to have eight electrons — an octet — in their valence shells, i.e. the configuration of the nearest noble gas.

**Significance.** It gives the first electronic explanation of valence and of why atoms combine at all; it accounts for the formulae of a great many compounds and lets Lewis dot structures be written; and it works well for most organic compounds and for the second-period elements.

**Limitations.**

1. *Incomplete octet of the central atom* — in \(\text{LiCl}\), \(\text{BeH}_2\), \(\text{BCl}_3\), \(\text{AlCl}_3\) and \(\text{BF}_3\) the central atom has fewer than eight electrons, because Li, Be and B have only 1, 2 and 3 valence electrons.
2. *Odd-electron molecules* — in \(\text{NO}\) and \(\text{NO}_2\) the total number of electrons is odd, so the octet cannot be satisfied for all the atoms.
3. *Expanded octet* — elements of the third period and beyond have \(3d\) orbitals available, so more than eight electrons can surround the central atom, as in \(\text{PF}_5\), \(\text{SF}_6\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\).
4. The rule is based on the inertness of the noble gases, yet xenon and krypton do form compounds such as \(\text{XeF}_2\), \(\text{KrF}_2\) and \(\text{XeOF}_2\).
5. It does not account for the SHAPE of a molecule.
6. It says nothing about the ENERGY of a molecule, so it cannot explain the relative stability of molecules.

The formation of an ionic compound depends on how easily the ions form and on how much energy is released when they pack into a lattice, so the favourable factors are:

1. **Low ionization enthalpy of the metal.** Forming the cation is always an endothermic step, so the smaller the ionization enthalpy the more easily the cation forms.
2. **High negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal.** The more energy released when the gaseous atom accepts an electron, the more easily the anion forms.
3. **High lattice enthalpy.** This is the decisive factor. The lattice enthalpy is the energy required to separate one mole of the solid ionic compound completely into its gaseous ions, and the energy released when the lattice forms is what makes the whole process favourable.

The chapter's own example makes the point: for NaCl the ionization enthalpy of Na is \(+495.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and the electron gain enthalpy of Cl is \(-348.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), so the two together are \(+147.1\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) — an energy COST. This is more than compensated by the enthalpy of lattice formation, \(-788\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and it is this that stabilises the crystal.

So a qualitative measure of the stability of an ionic compound is its enthalpy of lattice formation, not simply the achieving of an octet in the gaseous ions. Small, highly charged ions give large lattice enthalpies and hence favour ionic bonding.

In the VSEPR model the shape follows from the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom, the pairs arranging themselves so as to minimise repulsion (lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp).

- **\(\text{BeCl}_2\)** — Be has 2 valence electrons, both used in bonding: 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs (\(\text{AB}_2\)). Shape **linear**, Cl–Be–Cl \(= 180^\circ\).
- **\(\text{BCl}_3\)** — 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs (\(\text{AB}_3\)). Shape **trigonal planar**, Cl–B–Cl \(= 120^\circ\).
- **\(\text{SiCl}_4\)** — 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs (\(\text{AB}_4\)). Shape **tetrahedral**, Cl–Si–Cl \(= 109.5^\circ\).
- **\(\text{AsF}_5\)** — 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs (\(\text{AB}_5\)). Shape **trigonal bipyramidal**: three equatorial bonds at \(120^\circ\) and two axial bonds at \(90^\circ\) to the equatorial plane.
- **\(\text{H}_2\text{S}\)** — S has 6 valence electrons, two used in bonding: 2 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs (\(\text{AB}_2\text{E}_2\)). The four pairs are arranged tetrahedrally but the shape is **bent (angular)**, the H–S–H angle being pushed below \(109.5^\circ\) by the two lone pairs.
- **\(\text{PH}_3\)** — P has 5 valence electrons, three used in bonding: 3 bond pairs, 1 lone pair (\(\text{AB}_3\text{E}\)). The four pairs are arranged tetrahedrally but the shape is **trigonal pyramidal**, the H–P–H angle being pushed below \(109.5^\circ\) by the lone pair.

In both molecules the central atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised and the four electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally, so the ideal angle in each case would be \(109.5^\circ\). What differs is the NUMBER OF LONE PAIRS.

The repulsions fall in the order lone pair–lone pair \(>\) lone pair–bond pair \(>\) bond pair–bond pair, because a lone pair is localised on the central atom alone and so occupies more space than a bond pair, which is shared between two atoms.

- In \(\text{NH}_3\) nitrogen has **three bond pairs and one lone pair**. The single lone pair pushes the three N–H bond pairs closer together, reducing the angle from \(109.5^\circ\) to \(107^\circ\).
- In \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) oxygen has **two bond pairs and two lone pairs**. There are now two lone pairs repelling each other and repelling both bond pairs, so the compression is greater and the angle falls further, from \(109.5^\circ\) to \(104.5^\circ\).

Hence the bond angle in water \((104.5^\circ)\) is less than that in ammonia \((107^\circ)\), because water has one more lone pair than ammonia.

Bond order is the number of bonds — that is, the number of shared electron pairs — between two atoms in a molecule. It is 1 in \(\text{H}_2\), 2 in \(\text{O}_2\) and 3 in \(\text{N}_2\).

Bond strength is measured by the bond enthalpy, and the two are related as follows: **as the bond order increases, the bond enthalpy increases and the bond length decreases.** A higher bond order therefore means a shorter and stronger bond.

The chapter's own values show this:

- \(\text{H}_2\), bond order 1: \(\Delta_a H = 435.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), bond length \(74\,\text{pm}\)
- \(\text{O}_2\), bond order 2: \(\Delta_a H = 498\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), bond length \(121\,\text{pm}\)
- \(\text{N}_2\), bond order 3: \(\Delta_a H = 946\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), bond length \(109\,\text{pm}\)

So bond strength increases with bond order.

**Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms in a molecule.**

It is determined experimentally by spectroscopic, X-ray diffraction and electron-diffraction techniques.

Each atom of the bonded pair contributes to the bond length, and for a covalent bond the contribution of each atom is called its covalent radius — half the distance between two similar atoms joined by a covalent bond in the same molecule. Hence for a bond A–B,

\(R = r_A + r_B\)

where \(R\) is the bond length and \(r_A\), \(r_B\) are the covalent radii of A and B. For example the H–H bond length is \(74\,\text{pm}\) and the Cl–Cl bond length is \(199\,\text{pm}\).

A single Lewis structure for the carbonate ion shows one C=O double bond and two C–O single bonds, i.e. two different kinds of carbon–oxygen bond. Experimentally, **all three carbon–oxygen bonds in \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) are equivalent**, so no one Lewis structure describes the ion correctly.

The ion is therefore described as a **resonance hybrid** of three canonical forms which differ only in which of the three oxygen atoms carries the double bond. The important aspects of resonance that this illustrates are:

1. Resonance is invoked whenever a single Lewis structure cannot describe a species in agreement with its experimentally determined parameters.
2. The canonical (resonance) forms have **similar energies, the same positions of the nuclei**, and differ only in the distribution of bonding and non-bonding electron pairs.
3. The hybrid is **more stable** than any single canonical form, because the energy of the resonance hybrid is lower than that of any one contributing structure.
4. **Resonance averages the bond characteristics**, which is why all three C–O bonds in \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) come out identical and intermediate between a single and a double bond.
5. The canonical forms have **no real existence**. The ion does not spend part of its time as one form and part as another, there is no equilibrium between them (unlike keto–enol tautomerism), and the ion has one single structure — the hybrid — which simply cannot be drawn as one Lewis structure.

Resonance is indicated by a double-headed arrow between the canonical forms.

**No, they cannot be taken as canonical forms of a resonance hybrid.**

By definition, canonical (resonance) structures must have similar energies, **the same positions of the nuclei**, and must differ only in the distribution of the bonding and non-bonding electron pairs. Resonance is a redistribution of ELECTRONS only; no atom is allowed to move.

In the two structures given for \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\) the position of a hydrogen atom is different — in one it is bonded directly to phosphorus, in the other it is bonded to an oxygen atom. Since a nucleus has changed its place, the two are not canonical forms of one hybrid.

They are in fact **tautomers**: two distinct molecules in equilibrium with each other, interconverting by the migration of a hydrogen atom. The chapter makes exactly this distinction when it warns that there is no equilibrium between canonical forms of the kind that exists between the keto and enol tautomeric forms in tautomerism.

In each case the skeleton stays fixed and only the position of the multiple bond (and the associated lone pairs and formal charges) changes.

**\(\text{SO}_3\).** Sulphur is the central atom with three oxygens around it. There are three canonical forms, in each of which one S–O linkage is a double bond and the other two are single bonds carrying a negative formal charge on oxygen, with a \(+2\) formal charge on sulphur. Moving the double bond to each of the three oxygens in turn generates the three equivalent forms, and the hybrid has all three S–O bonds identical.

**\(\text{NO}_2\).** Two canonical forms, in which the N=O double bond and the N–O single bond are interchanged. Because \(\text{NO}_2\) has an odd total number of electrons, one unpaired electron remains on nitrogen in each form and the octet cannot be completed on every atom — the chapter itself cites \(\text{NO}_2\) as an odd-electron molecule for exactly this reason.

**\(\text{NO}_3^-\).** Nitrogen is central with three oxygens. There are three canonical forms in which the N=O double bond occupies each of the three N–O positions in turn; the two singly bonded oxygens carry a negative formal charge each and nitrogen carries \(+1\). All three N–O bonds in the hybrid are therefore equivalent.

[Note: the chapter draws resonance structures only for \(\text{O}_3\), \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) and \(\text{CO}_2\); these three are constructed by applying the same rules it states.]

In each case the metal atom loses its valence electrons and the non-metal atom gains them, both ions ending with a noble-gas configuration, and the ions are then held together by electrostatic attraction.

**(a) K and S.** Potassium has one valence electron and sulphur needs two, so two potassium atoms are required:

\(\text{K}\ ([\text{Ar}]4s^1) \rightarrow \text{K}^+\ ([\text{Ar}]) + e^-\) (twice)

\(\text{S}\ ([\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^4) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{S}^{2-}\ ([\text{Ar}])\)

\(2\text{K}^+ + \text{S}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{S}\)

In Lewis symbols, each K carries one dot which is transferred to sulphur; \(\text{K}^+\) is left with no dots and \([\text{S}]^{2-}\) carries eight.

**(b) Ca and O.**

\(\text{Ca}\ ([\text{Ar}]4s^2) \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+}\ ([\text{Ar}]) + 2e^-\)

\(\text{O}\ ([\text{He}]2s^2 2p^4) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\ ([\text{Ne}])\)

\(\text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CaO}\)

Calcium's two dots are transferred to oxygen, which goes from six dots to eight.

**(c) Al and N.**

\(\text{Al}\ ([\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1) \rightarrow \text{Al}^{3+}\ ([\text{Ne}]) + 3e^-\)

\(\text{N}\ ([\text{He}]2s^2 2p^3) + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{N}^{3-}\ ([\text{Ne}])\)

\(\text{Al}^{3+} + \text{N}^{3-} \rightarrow \text{AlN}\)

Aluminium's three dots are transferred to nitrogen, which goes from five dots to eight.

For a polyatomic molecule the dipole moment is the **vector sum** of the individual bond dipoles, so it depends on the spatial arrangement of the bonds as well as on their polarity. Measuring the dipole moment therefore tells us the shape.

**\(\text{CO}_2\).** Each C=O bond is polar, yet the measured dipole moment of \(\text{CO}_2\) is **zero**. Two equal bond dipoles can add to zero only if they are exactly opposed, i.e. only if the O=C=O arrangement is **linear** with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\). The two bond moments then cancel exactly.

**\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).** Each O–H bond is polar, and the measured dipole moment is **\(1.85\,\text{D}\)** \((6.17 \times 10^{-30}\,\text{C m})\) — clearly not zero. If the molecule were linear the two equal O–H bond dipoles would cancel and the resultant would be zero, which contradicts the measurement. The two bonds must therefore be inclined to each other, and the resultant of two bond dipoles at \(104.5^\circ\) accounts for the observed value.

Hence \(\text{CO}_2\) is linear and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is bent, even though both are triatomic.

Dipole moment, \(\mu = Q \times r\), is the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance separating the centres of positive and negative charge. It is a vector, expressed in debye units \((1\,\text{D} = 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\,\text{C m})\), and it is useful in the following ways.

1. **It distinguishes polar from non-polar molecules.** A molecule with \(\mu = 0\) is non-polar; a non-zero \(\mu\) means the molecule is polar. \(\text{H}_2\) has \(\mu = 0\), HF has \(\mu = 1.78\,\text{D}\).
2. **It gives the shape and symmetry of a molecule.** Because the molecular dipole moment is the vector sum of the bond dipoles, a zero value for a molecule with polar bonds proves a symmetrical arrangement in which the bond moments cancel — \(\text{CO}_2\) \((\mu = 0)\) is linear, \(\text{BF}_3\) \((\mu = 0)\) is trigonal planar and \(\text{CCl}_4\) \((\mu = 0)\) is tetrahedral, whereas \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) \((1.85\,\text{D})\) is bent and \(\text{NH}_3\) \((1.47\,\text{D})\) is pyramidal.
3. **It measures the extent of polarity of a bond**, and hence the percentage ionic character of a bond, since a larger charge separation gives a larger \(\mu\).
4. **It distinguishes between closely related molecules** and reveals the contribution of a lone pair. \(\text{NH}_3\) \((1.47\,\text{D})\) and \(\text{NF}_3\) \((0.23\,\text{D})\) have the same shape, and the difference shows that in \(\text{NH}_3\) the lone-pair orbital dipole adds to the resultant bond moment while in \(\text{NF}_3\) it opposes it.

[Note: the chapter does not print a list under the heading "applications of dipole moment"; the four uses above are the ones it actually makes of the quantity.]

**Electronegativity** is the tendency of an atom **in a chemical bond** to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It is a relative quantity expressed on an arbitrary scale, so it is a pure number with no units, and it cannot be measured directly for a single atom.

**Electron gain enthalpy**, \(\Delta_{eg}H\), is the enthalpy change when a **gas-phase atom in its ground state** gains an electron:

\(\text{X}(g) + e^- \rightarrow \text{X}^-(g)\)

**How they differ.**

1. Electronegativity refers to an atom that is BONDED to another atom; electron gain enthalpy refers to an ISOLATED atom in the gaseous state.
2. Electronegativity concerns a shared electron pair being pulled towards one atom; electron gain enthalpy concerns the complete transfer of an electron to the atom.
3. Electronegativity is a relative, dimensionless number; electron gain enthalpy is an energy, measured in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and it can be positive or negative.
4. Electronegativity has a fixed value for an atom only in a given bonding situation; electron gain enthalpy is a definite experimental property of the element.

[Note: this chapter does not itself define electronegativity — it uses the term once and refers the reader to Unit 3. Only the definition of electron gain enthalpy above is taken from this chapter.]

When a covalent bond is formed between two **similar** atoms — as in \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{O}_2\), \(\text{Cl}_2\), \(\text{N}_2\) or \(\text{F}_2\) — the shared pair is attracted equally by both nuclei and sits exactly midway between them. Such a bond is a **non-polar covalent bond**.

When the two atoms are **dissimilar**, the more electronegative atom attracts the shared pair more strongly, so the electron pair is displaced towards it. The bond then has one end slightly negative and the other slightly positive, and it is called a **polar covalent bond**.

**Example — HF.** Fluorine is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pair lies closer to fluorine. Fluorine acquires a fractional negative charge and hydrogen a fractional positive charge:

\(\text{H}^{\delta+} - \text{F}^{\delta-}\)

The resulting separation of charge gives HF a dipole moment of \(1.78\,\text{D}\), whereas \(\text{H}_2\) has a dipole moment of zero. In chemistry this polarity is shown by a crossed arrow drawn on the Lewis structure, the cross at the positive end and the arrowhead at the negative end.

The ionic character of a bond increases with the **difference in electronegativity** between the two bonded atoms. Where the two atoms are identical the shared pair is attracted equally and the bond has no ionic character at all.

- **\(\text{N}_2\)** — a homonuclear molecule, so the electronegativity difference is exactly zero and the bond is purely covalent. It is the least ionic of the five.
- **\(\text{SO}_2\)** and **\(\text{ClF}_3\)** — both are bonds between two non-metals with a moderate electronegativity difference (S–O and Cl–F). On the Pauling scale both differences work out the same, \(\approx 1.0\).
- **\(\text{K}_2\text{O}\)** — a bond between a highly electropositive alkali metal and a highly electronegative non-metal, difference \(\approx 2.7\).
- **LiF** — the largest difference of all, \(\approx 3.0\), between the most electronegative element and an alkali metal.

Increasing order of ionic character:

\(\text{N}_2 < \text{SO}_2 \approx \text{ClF}_3 < \text{K}_2\text{O} < \text{LiF}\)

[Note: this chapter tabulates no electronegativity values — it refers the reader to Unit 3 — so the numerical differences above come from the Pauling scale and not from this chapter. On those values \(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{ClF}_3\) have the same electronegativity difference, so nothing in this chapter separates them; many sources place \(\text{ClF}_3\) immediately above \(\text{SO}_2\).]

Acetic acid has \(2(4) + 4(1) + 2(6) = 24\) valence electrons, i.e. 12 electron pairs to distribute.

**What is wrong with the structure as printed.**

1. A **hydrogen atom is shown joined to carbon by a double bond**. Hydrogen has only one valence electron and needs only a duplet, so it can form exactly ONE covalent bond. That linkage must be a single bond. As drawn, the methyl carbon would also carry five bonds and so exceed its octet.
2. The **carbon–oxygen bond of the carboxyl group is drawn as a single bond**. With only three single bonds that carbon has six electrons and its octet is incomplete, so this linkage must be a **double bond, C=O**.

**The correct Lewis structure.** The methyl carbon is joined to three hydrogen atoms and to the second carbon, all by single bonds. The second carbon is joined to the methyl carbon by a single bond, to one oxygen by a **double bond**, and to the second oxygen by a single bond; that second oxygen is joined to a hydrogen atom. The doubly bonded oxygen carries **two lone pairs** and the hydroxyl oxygen also carries **two lone pairs**.

Check: 7 bonds share \(3(2) + 2 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 16\) electrons, and the four lone pairs account for the remaining 8 — 24 in all. Every carbon and both oxygens now have a complete octet, and every hydrogen a duplet.
